title: Revealing and reducing growth-induced interfacial disorder in preferentially aligned nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond
authors: Cheng-I Ho, Marina Davydova, Patrik Straňák, Felix Hoffmann, Peter Knittel, Andrej Denisenko, Jörg Wrachtrup
abstract: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in chemical-vapor-deposition (CVD) diamond can form preferentially oriented ensembles with high sensing performance and low densities of lattice defects. Thin films of this material are a cornerstone of various imaging modalities. However, nitrogen injection needed to produce such films can transiently drive growth out of equilibrium, generating interfacial strain and spin defects that degrade NV coherence. Here, we investigate this disorder in $^{12}\text{C}$-enriched, preferentially oriented NV layers grown on (111) diamond using two nitrogen-injection procedures, combined with nanometer-scale selective plasma etching and NV spin-coherence measurements. Pulsed nitrogen injection produces a pronounced nitrogen overshoot within a 60--80 nm interfacial region, generating excessive amounts of defects. By contrast, smooth nitrogen delivery through mass flow controllers substantially suppresses interfacial disorder, yielding coherence properties close to the theoretical limit imposed by spin-bath noise. A 50-nm NV layer is used to demonstrate proton nuclear magnetic resonance detection. This work reveals the role of interfacial disorder associated with the nitrogen-doping procedure and provides a route to growing high-quality, thin NV-doped layers for quantum-sensing applications.
summary: This research tackles the critical issue of growth-induced disorder in NV centers within diamond used for quantum sensing. By comparing pulsed versus smooth nitrogen doping methods, the authors demonstrate that controlled doping procedures are essential to minimize interfacial strain and defects. This leads to high-quality layers capable of achieving near-theoretical coherence limits and enabling sensitive NMR detection.
main_problem: The study investigates how growth-induced interfacial disorder, stemming from nitrogen doping procedures during CVD diamond growth, degrades the coherence of Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers.
main_result: Smooth nitrogen delivery significantly suppresses this interfacial disorder, leading to NV spin-coherence properties approaching theoretical limits. The work also successfully demonstrated proton NMR detection using these high-quality layers.
method: The researchers compared two nitrogen injection methods (pulsed vs. smooth) and used advanced characterization techniques like ODMR spectroscopy, ToF-SIMS depth profiling, and step-etching to map disorder gradients.
model_or_system: The physical system is NV centers embedded in $^12	ext{C}$-enriched diamond thin films grown on (111) substrates. The analysis focuses on the impact of nitrogen concentration profiles and resulting lattice strain/defects on spin coherence.
key_observables: NV spin-coherence decay rates ($\Gamma^*_2$, $\Gamma_{	ext{DQR}}^2$), Nitrogen concentration profiles ([N]), P1 center concentrations ([P1]), and NMR signal detection capability.
important_parameters: Interfacial disorder magnitude, nitrogen doping procedure type (pulsed vs. smooth), effective depth ($d_{NV}$), and the resulting coherence time limit imposed by spin-bath noise.
main_assumptions: The analysis often approximates the total decay rate as a sum of contributions ($\Gamma^*_2 \approx \Gamma_{	ext{DQR}}^2 + \Gamma_{	ext{strain}}$) and assumes certain background contributions are minor for simplification.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate OES/ToF-SIMS profiles comparing doping methods, ODMR spectra showing decay rates across etched layers (R0-R3), and final results summarizing concentration gradients and NMR detection signals.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares two growth procedures using multiple characterization tools (OES, ToF-SIMS) to quantify disorder. It then uses step-etching and spin-coherence measurements across depth profiles to correlate doping history with quantum performance, culminating in a demonstration of high-sensitivity sensing.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it directly addresses material science limitations (growth defects) that impede the realization of solid-state quantum sensors, bridging condensed matter physics with quantum optics/sensing.
